question.prompt: At a math contest, \(57\) students are wearing blue shirts, and another \(75\) students are wearing yellow shirts. The \(132\) students are assigned into \(66\) pairs. In exactly \(23\) of these pairs, both students are wearing blue shirts. In how many pairs are both students wearing yellow shirts?

solutions.title: Find the mixed pairs first
solutions.explanation:
Any blue-shirted student outside the all-blue pairs must have a yellow-shirted partner, so counting the remaining blue students determines the mixed pairs.

The \(23\) all-blue pairs contain \(2\cdot23=46\) blue-shirted students. This leaves \(57-46=11\) blue-shirted students, each in a different mixed pair. These mixed pairs therefore use exactly \(11\) yellow-shirted students.

The remaining \(75-11=64\) yellow-shirted students all belong to all-yellow pairs. Each pair contains two students, so the number of all-yellow pairs is
\[
\frac{64}{2}=\boxed{32},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

solutions.title: Compare the color totals
solutions.explanation:
Mixed pairs contain equal numbers of the two colors, so they contribute nothing to the difference between the yellow and blue totals.

There are \(75-57=18\) more yellow-shirted students than blue-shirted students. Each all-yellow pair contributes \(2\) to this difference, while each all-blue pair contributes \(-2\). Thus there must be \(18/2=9\) more all-yellow pairs than all-blue pairs.

Since there are \(23\) all-blue pairs, the number of all-yellow pairs is
\[
23+9=\boxed{32},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
